name: secrets-management
context: An estate in which credentials - database passwords, API keys, OAuth client secrets, SSH keys, encryption keys - live in source repositories, environment variables, CI variables and config files. Once a secret reaches any of those it is in history and in logs indefinitely, so it can only be replaced, never revoked. Secrets management is the architectural response: move the whole credential lifecycle - creation, storage, distribution, rotation, revocation, audit - into a hardened vault, bootstrap access to that vault with a platform identity so no secret is needed in order to fetch a secret, and prefer short-lived dynamic credentials over stored passwords wherever the target system can mint them.
benefits: Revocation becomes possible at all. This is the capability that an env-var or git-committed secret fundamentally lacks, and it is what makes an actual incident response possible rather than just a credential replacement

Dynamic secrets shrink the attack window. Vault's database secrets engine generates a user against a lease and destroys it when the lease expires, so a credential leaked a year ago has long since ceased to exist
Eliminates secret sprawl and bounds blast radius. Path-scoped policies mean a compromised component reaches only its own secrets, and access is attributable to one identity in an audit trail
Automated rotation with a dual-key transition window turns rotation from the most-deferred task in security into a routine pipeline, without the outage that manual rotation causes

The transit engine and envelope encryption keep data-encryption keys inside the vault or an HSM: a leaked database dump is ciphertext, and re-keying means rotating one master key rather than rewriting a table
Every read, write, rotation and revocation is recorded, producing audit evidence without a separate instrumentation project
Solves the secret-zero bootstrap problem by authenticating to the vault with a Kubernetes ServiceAccount, a cloud IAM role or an OIDC identity, so no long-lived vault token is stored anywhere
tradeoffs: The vault is a Tier-0 dependency. Its unavailability can block service startup and dynamic credential renewal, cascading into a system-wide outage - which is why HA, deliberate TTLs and a defined degraded mode are mandatory, not optional

Centralization is not automatically the right answer for every secret. A dynamic database credential that forces a restart on each rotation can break long-lived sessions such as SSO; mature estates deliberately keep some secrets on simpler rails and move them only when the evidence supports it

Every application must implement token acquisition, renewal before TTL expiry, retry on transient vault errors, and a caching policy. That is real distributed-systems work, and the renewal path is the one that fails silently at 3am

Dynamic secrets require the vault to hold a network path to the managed resource and its own privileged root account in that system - a new high-value credential, which is why Vault's own guidance is a 1:1 relationship between a root user and a secrets engine, and to rotate it immediately

Performance: an API call per decrypt or per credential fetch is fine at startup and unacceptable on a hot path, so agents and caches get introduced - and the cache then becomes the thing that must be secured
Creating and deleting database users on every rotation can take table locks at scale; static roles exist precisely to avoid that, at the cost of per-workload isolation

Environment variables are still the most convenient delivery mechanism and remain a regression: they leak via /proc/self/environ and crash dumps, so 'just inject it as an env var' reintroduces the exposure the vault was adopted to remove
Nothing forces hygiene automatically. Without a baseline expiry policy, secrets are created with no owner and no expiry window and simply accumulate
use_cases: Issuing a per-workload database user with a 24-hour lease instead of one shared application password
Bootstrapping vault access from a Kubernetes ServiceAccount so no vault token is ever stored in the repository
Keeping PII column encryption keys inside the vault so only ciphertext reaches the application database
Automating credential rotation end to end so a rotation reaches running pods with no human in the loop
avoid_when: The estate has no capacity to operate a highly available control-plane service - the outage risk exceeds the leak risk it mitigates
Credentials are already short-lived and minted by the target system itself, so a vault adds a dependency without removing one
The application cannot be changed to fetch at startup and renew on TTL; a vault with no renewal logic fails silently at expiry
The deployment has no trustworthy platform identity, because that leaves a stored vault token as the only bootstrap option
component_types: Secrets engine (KV, database, transit, PKI, OIDC)
Auth method bound to platform identity
Sidecar injector / CSI driver / External Secrets Operator
technology_stack: HashiCorp Vault (dynamic secrets, leases, transit, key management engine)
AWS Secrets Manager / Azure Key Vault / GCP Secret Manager
anti_patterns: One master secret shared by dozens of services with no segmentation: a leak in one place compromises all of them at once and cannot be attributed
Postponing rotation indefinitely because automation is judged risky - manual rotation is what actually becomes an expired-credential outage
Storing secrets in environment variables and calling that management; /proc/self/environ and crash dumps expose them
Bootstrapping the vault with a long-lived token committed to the repository, which defers secret zero rather than solving it
Creating and deleting a database user on every rotation instead of using static roles, where user churn causes table locks
Issuing secrets with no baseline policy requiring an owner, resource tag and expiry window
A break-glass path with no mandatory audit and no TTL - the rare exception hardens into a permanent bypass
Assuming client-side TTL caching is free, when the cache is now the most valuable target in the pod
design_principles: Design for revocation, not replacement: a secret written anywhere else can only ever be replaced
Short-lived beats well-hidden - prefer dynamic credentials with a TTL to a stored password, wherever the target can mint them
Bootstrap with identity, not with secrets, so the chain of trust has no static root credential in application hands
Scope every secret to exactly one consumer; isolation boundaries cost little and blast-radius analysis costs a great deal
Treat the credential path as a distributed system: acquisition, renewal, retry and caching are explicit design work
The vault is an availability dependency - its failure mode is designed, not assumed away
best_practices: Use one secrets engine mount point per application, isolating policy, root credentials and lifecycle management
Point the vault at a single client-facing VIP or FQDN per backend so database failover does not require multiple mounts
Start with generous lease TTLs (24-48 hours) and tighten from measured renewal behaviour; prune dangling leases, which consume memory
Use static roles where user create/delete churn would lock tables, and dynamic roles where per-workload isolation is worth a restart
Deliver through an agent, sidecar or CSI driver rather than environment variables, and close the loop with a reloader that rolls workloads when the secret changes
Automatically unseal from KMS or HSM and reserve Shamir's secret sharing for the offline root only
Authenticate to the vault with Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, cloud IAM roles or OIDC, so the vault's own credential is not a stored secret
Issue encryption as a service from the transit engine so data keys never reach the application or the database
Rehearse rotation: trigger it manually, confirm the new credential works and the old one is genuinely rejected
